subject: Trump declares ceasefire with Iran ‘over’
body: Plus, US rare earths flow to Asia, and Santander axes top China banker ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ All newsletters | Read this in your browser Benjamin Wilhelm Newsletter Editor ‌ ‌ July 9 2026 Good morning and welcome to FirstFT. In today’s newsletter: * Trump says US-Iran ceasefire is ‘over’ * Chinese economist who doubted official GDP data dies * The price of Palantir’s politics * Japan’s borrowing costs soar to 30-year high ‌ The US has begun striking Iran for the second night in a row, hours after Donald Trump said he considered the ceasefire between Washington and Tehran “over”. What’s happening: US forces “have started conducting additional strikes against Iran to further degrade their ability to threaten freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz”, US Central Command, which oversees American military operations in the Middle East, said on Wednesday. Oil prices rose by the most in two months on the flare-up of tensions. Brent crude extended gains to be up 6.6 per cent in after-hours trading on Wednesday at $79.06 a barrel. The international benchmark had earlier risen as much as 8.7 per cent to $80.59. Speaking about the ceasefire at the Nato summit in Ankara earlier in the day, the US president told reporters: “As far as I’m concerned, it’s over.” Trump lashed out at Iran’s leaders, calling them “scum” and “sick people” — some of his most bellicose language since Tehran and Washington last month agreed to extend the truce and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Trump also said the US might reinstate its naval blockade on Iran’s ports, only targeting Iranian ships, or attempt to take control of the vital oil hub of Kharg Island. However, Trump suggested after the conclusion of the two-day summit that any military exchanges would end “quickly” — and that the US would not return to a full-blown war with Iran. Inflation threat: Renewed conflict in the Middle East would drive up global inflation, damage supply chains and weigh on financial markets, the IMF warned, as it lifted its forecasts for price growth. In a report finalised before Trump said the ceasefire with Iran was over, the fund said that while the global economy had weathered the conflict in the Middle East better than expected so far, the threat of fresh hostilities “looms large”. * Go deeper: Trump’s push to get ships moving through the Strait of Hormuz keeps colliding with Tehran’s resistance to cede control. Here’s why the US and Iran are stuck in a cycle of tit-for-tat strikes. * More from Ankara: Trump said the US would grant Ukraine a licence to produce Patriot surface-to-air interceptor missiles, agreeing to a significant request from Kyiv. Nato allies are cautiously optimistic that the US president had made a significant shift in favour of Kyiv. Here’s what else I’m keeping tabs on today: * Economic data: China publishes June inflation data. * Monetary policy decision: Malaysia’s central bank is expected to keep its policy rate unchanged at 2.75 per cent. FIVE MORE TOP STORIES 1. US rare earths produced by Washington-backed companies are flowing to Japan and South Korea, as American demand has yet to materialise despite the Trump administration’s push to develop a national supply chain. Read the full story. 2. The death of a prominent Chinese economist who openly questioned official GDP data has prompted an outpouring of mourning for a figure many saw as a “daring truth teller” in a country intolerant of independent voices. Gao Shanwen, former economist of SDIC Securities, a government-controlled investment group, died at the age of 55 “due to illness”, state media reported. 3. Santander has overhauled its Asia-Pacific business under new management, removing its top banker in Beijing, tightening employee oversight and scrapping perks such as free breakfasts. The Spanish lender has shaken up its corporate and investment bank in the region under Alberto Rivero, who took over as head of Asia Pacific at the start of the year, according to people familiar with the matter. 4. South Korean stocks have entered a technical bear market as investors raise concerns about the long-term prospects of the AI chipmakers that have driven a world-beating rally. The Kospi index is down more than 20 per cent from its record high in June after slipping more than 5 per cent on Wednesday. * Indonesian stock market: S&P Dow Jones Indices has warned of a possible downgrade of Indonesia to a frontier market, following a similar warning from rival index provider MSCI. 5. Temasek has set out plans to nearly triple its exposure to AI companies and double its private credit holdings over the next five years, as Singapore’s state investor focuses on accelerating returns after several lacklustre years. In a bid to turbocharge growth, Temasek announced plans on Wednesday to increase its exposure to AI companies from 6 per cent of its total portfolio to 15 per cent by 2031. THE PRICE OF PALANTIR’S POLITICS © FT montage/Getty Images In the years following its founding in 2003 with a mission to help defend the west from another 9/11-style terrorist attack, Palantir single-handedly revolutionised the US defence industry. In the intervening years the technology company has saved lives on the battlefield and in the Covid-19 pandemic. But Palantir’s enthusiastic embrace of Donald Trump’s policies and its defence of Israel’s war in Gaza have spurred protests and political outrage as well as unease among staff. Is Palantir too tied to Trump? WE’RE ALSO READING . . . * China needs another Zhu Rongji: The country’s manufacturing glut has revived memories of sweeping reforms under the charismatic reformist premier, writes Edward White. * The joy of tangible media: Sony’s plan to drop physical discs endangers the company and its customers, writes Brooke Masters. * Beijing’s AI supply chain efforts: State-backed CXMT has been thrust into the global spotlight by the race for memory chips and interest from Apple. CHART OF THE DAY Japan’s borrowing costs have shot to their highest in 30 years as investors fret over the tumbling yen and the effect of a $2tn long-term spending plan on the country’s massive debts. body: Fresh inflation fears as war reignites, Palantir’s politics, AI glasses ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ All newsletters | Read this in your browser Darren Dodd Writer and Commissioning Editor ‌ ‌ July 8 2026 TODAY’S TOP NEWS STORIES * Donald Trump said the US-Iran ceasefire was “over” following renewed military strikes between the two countries. Get the latest in our live Nato blog. * Trump said the US would grant Ukraine a licence to produce Patriot surface-to-air interceptor missiles, agreeing to a significant request from Kyiv. * Apple pledged $30bn to buy billions of US-made chips from Broadcom, as the iPhone maker continues to woo the Trump administration. ‌ Good evening. Here we go again. Oil prices are climbing after the renewal of hostilities in the Middle East, causing traders to up their bets on interest rate rises. And that was before a report from the IMF this afternoon highlighting the susceptibility of the global economy to a fresh surge in inflation. Oil prices rose more than 5 per cent to top $78 per barrel as the US-Iran clashes escalated, while global stocks fell and analysts adjusted their timelines for rate cuts. A quarter-point rise by the US Federal Reserve is now expected by October, and from the European Central Bank by September – both earlier than previously expected. In the UK, a Bank of England quarter-point rate rise is now fully priced in by the end of the year. In its World Economic Outlook, finalised before today’s events in the Middle East, the IMF said that while the global economy had weathered the conflict better than expected so far, the threat of fresh hostilities “looms large”. The Fund predicted global inflation would increase from 4.1 per cent in 2025 to 4.7 per cent this year — higher than it estimated in April — before falling back to 3.9 per cent in 2027. Global growth will retreat from 3.5 per cent in 2025 to 3 per cent this year, marginally weaker than previously predicted, before bouncing back to 3.4 per cent in 2027, the IMF said. It warned that renewed conflict would drive up commodity prices and worsen supply shortages as well as exchange rate pressures. The release of oil inventories had helped ease the shock in energy markets, it said, but these were now approaching multiyear lows and “could reach stress levels should supply disruptions persist or hoarding gather steam”. Food security could also be under threat. Separately the IMF named former Bank of England policymaker Silvana Tenreyro as its next chief economist. She had been viewed as one of the most dovish members of the BoE rate-setting body, despite the UK suffering from its worst bout of inflation in decades. Her predecessor Pierre-Olivier Gourinchas told the FT recently that “tit-for-tat” trade warfare was another big threat to the global economy. With globalisation in retreat, countries were increasingly imposing trade barriers or exploiting “chokepoints”, such as Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz, for political gains, he said. ‌ QUOTE OF THE DAY By 2026, if you are choosing to work at Palantir, you are making an active statement about your own politics. They have become the place for Republican tech bros to go work. A former employee says the most prized thing in Silicon Valley is to be a former Palantirian: enjoying the pedigree without the stigma. Our Big Read considers whether pushback to the tech group’s politics threatens the core of its $330bn business. ‌ ECONOMICS * Nato allies have unveiled billions of dollars of defence deals even as Donald Trump threatened to pull all US troops out of Europe. * A new online system to pre-authorise entry to the EU is set to be delayed until next year, after the chaotic rollout of electronic border checks. * German business warned of a “lost decade” on concerns that €10bn in tax cuts may not be enough to jump-start the country’s stagnant economy. * Europe must have the financial power to match its economic heft, writes former Italian prime minister Enrico Letta in the FT. * Presumptive PM Andy Burnham needs to tackle “unsustainable” public finances quickly to minimise economic risks, the UK’s fiscal watchdog warned. * Companies’ use of non-compete clauses is dragging down productivity in rich economies, according to new OECD research. * South Africa’s treasury is withholding state funds from Johannesburg and elsewhere for a month in a bid to stop wasteful spending ahead of local polls. * Simmering discord between Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto and the country’s top businessmen threatens a spillover effect on to the economy. ‌ MARKETS * US rare earths produced by Washington-backed companies are flowing to Japan and South Korea, as American demand has yet to materialise. * The value of bids for companies on the London Stock Exchange is 27 times greater than the value of new entrants so far this year, raising fresh fears about the shrinking of the UK’s public markets. * Japan’s borrowing costs have shot to their highest level in 30 years, as investors fret over the tumbling yen and a revival in inflation. ‌ CHART OF THE DAY European policymakers are under pressure to prepare for increasingly deadly conditions on the fastest-warming continent. The FT’s network of reporters compares approaches to the new world of extreme heat. ‌ BUSINESS * Santander has overhauled its Asia-Pacific business under new management, including removing its top banker in Beijing, the FT revealed. * Italy’s UniCredit secured a 47.6 per cent holding in Commerzbank, bringing it within striking distance of taking control of Germany’s second-largest lender. * HSBC is halting lending to riskier private credit clients, after high-profile bankruptcies cast doubt on underwriting standards in the sector. * Europe’s top banking watchdogs warned that frontier AI models such as Anthropic’s Mythos pose “systemic risks to the financial system”. * The Bank of England announced plans to ease a key capital requirement for UK banks despite concerns that it will add to risks in the financial system. * Meta is testing “super sensing” AI glasses that would use cameras and audio recordings to capture a wearer’s every moment. Meta also launched its first image generation model since the overhaul of its AI organisation. * Tesco is exploring a sale of its central and eastern European operations in a move that would end its attempts to build a global retail empire. ‌ TRADE * Greek shipping companies have made at least $3.8bn transporting Russian oil over the past three years, the FT revealed. * The world’s biggest freight forwarder said land routes to take goods to the Gulf were not a sustainable alternative to voyages through the Strait of Hormuz. ‌ SOME GOOD NEWS ‌ ‌ Small satellites would detect nuclear arms launched secretly into orbit under a new monitoring system proposed by a scientist to address fears about the militarisation of space. This is how the sharpest minds in tech characterize an AI agent: Bill Gates' definition: - Proactive (acts without being asked what to do next) - Cross-application (operates across multiple systems) - Improves over time (learns from experience) a16z's definition: - Complex planning (breaks down a goal into multi-step sequences) - Interaction with outside systems (actually calls APIs, clicks buttons, reads data—not just generates text) Sequoia's definition: - Dispatched autonomously (you tell it the goal, not the steps) - Recovers from failure (if an API times out, it retries intelligently) - Persists until job is done (doesn't give up after one attempt) This is how Crew AI’s founder João describes AI agents: An agent is an autonomous unit that can: - Scan its environment. - Uses tools to accomplish objectives. - Maintains memory of interactions. - Makes decisions based on its role and goal - Communicates, collaborates, and delegates. - Recovers and adapts from feedback All four are saying the same thing: An agent is a system that can plan, act, and adapt without human intervention at each step. What is not an Agent? Custom GPTs Aren't Agents. You describe what you want it to do. It generates text based on that description. Text-in, text-out. ChatGPT isn't an Agent. Neither is Claude. It can reason through problems. It can write code, draft emails, and explain quantum physics. But it can’t execute anything itself (not yet, at least). The Automation-Wrapped-in-LLM isn’t an Agent. He calls a regional sales lead, who mentions a local influencer just wore the shoe on Instagram. He eyeballs it, picks a number, emails the factory. If he’s wrong, it's expensive either way. Too high, and the brand discounts unsold inventory three months later. Too low, and the shoe sells out in six days while customers buy a competitor's pair instead. The planner learns about it 14 days later. Post-Agents Now picture 2026, same brand, an agent doing the job. It checks sell-through data in real time, and flags the influencer post the moment it happens. It then calculates next week's number, validates that the number is within budget and inventory restrictions and sends it straight to the factory. If Chicago starts selling twice as fast as predicted mid-week, the agent doesn't wait for Sunday; it adjusts, reroutes inventory, and flags the change with its reasoning attached. He's not pulling and guessing anymore. He's reviewing the agent's call and overriding it when his judgment catches something the data doesn't know yet. The Core Foundational Zones of an AI Agent How builders should actually think about it: 1. Scans Its Environment (Perception Zone) The agent scans its environment (what the current state is, what data is available, and what tools it can access). Sneaker Example: It reads real-time sell-through, regional weather, and social mentions across every store. 2. Maintains Memory of Interactions (Memory Zone) The agent remembers what happened before, so it doesn't repeat mistakes or re-learn the same context. Sneaker Example: It remembers last week's forecast and how actual sales diverged from it. 3. Makes Decisions Based on Its Role and Goal (Reasoning Zone) The agent decomposes the goal into steps and plans. Sneaker Example: Goal = "Set next week's production number" → weigh sell-through, weather, and social signals → decide the number. 4. Uses Tools to Accomplish Objectives (Action Zone) The agent actually performs tasks such as calling APIs, updating databases, and executing code. Without this zone, it's just a smart chatbot. Example: It sends the production number straight to the factory's ordering system. 5. Recovers and Adapts from Feedback (Feedback Zone). The agent observes the outcome and adjusts (retries, escalates, or tries another approach) if something's off. Sneaker Example: Chicago sells twice as fast as predicted, so it revises the number mid-week and flags the change with its reasoning. 6. Communicates, Collaborates, and Delegates (Collaboration Zone) It shares context with other agents, hands off subtasks when another agent (or human) is better suited for them. Sneaker Example: The forecasting agent doesn't reroute Chicago's inventory itself. It delegates that to a logistics agent, while flagging the demand spike to a pricing agent that decides whether to adjust markdowns elsewhere. This loop: Perception → Memory → Reasoning → Action → Feedback → Collaboration is what separates an agent from everything else. subject: Working It: Is the legal sector fit for humans?
body: Burnout and badly behaved colleagues lead to industry brain drain ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ All newsletters | Read this in your browser Isabel Berwick Working It Editor ‌ ‌ July 8 2026 Hello and welcome to Working It, the FT’s weekly guide to the workplace and leadership. The changing shape of working life, post-50, is the (non-AI) work trend to watch. Factors such as falling birth rates, longer “healthspans” of being fit and active, as well as economic instability, mean many people are working for longer 🏃🏻‍♂️. There is also freedom and flexibility aplenty during this “third act”: the landscape is evolving. Last week, FT HQ hosted a (very) full house of alumni from our FT Board Director programme, discussing “third acts” after executive life. An expert panel talked about non-executive director opportunities, becoming an entrepreneur (older founders are more successful !), volunteering, the role of purpose — and much more. Plus, smart employers increasingly value the “ROE”, or return on experience, that older workers bring — as coined by one of our panellists, 55/Redefined CEO Lyndsey Simpson. Nobody mentioned the “R-word”* If further proof of trend were needed, 2026 is the year of the “third act” book: Lyndsey and fellow panellist Lucy Standing have already published on the subject this year, plus there’s Longevity Nation, by US author Michael Clinton, and Lynda Gratton’s Living the 100-Year Life is coming in September. *Retirement [🤫]. Read on for a look at the cultural and workload pressures on lawyers. In short: is the system increasingly incompatible with being human in the 21st century? Do share your views: isabel.berwick@ft.com. IS THE LEGAL SECTOR BUILT FOR HUMANS? [AND WE AREN’T TALKING ABOUT AI] ‌ ‌ Too much, for too long? © FT montage/Dreamstime When social scientist Issac Lim, founder of Anthro Insights, ran a research study about lawyer retention in Singapore, he received 100 pages of free-text comments from some of the nearly 900 lawyers who took part. They “really let it go”, Issac says. “They really wanted to say something about what they were experiencing at work.” This included frustrations with ongoing tolerance of badly behaved colleagues who are also “rainmakers”, and so bring large amounts of income to the firm 🤬. “What comes out quite frequently in the study is that rainmakers sometimes get a pass,” Issac says. Some of the comments from older lawyers also suggested that the younger generation (termed “the strawberry generation” in Singapore) have it easy at work, although, as Issac points out, “every generation says the same of the generation after”. And while AI will change how lawyers work, Isaac says, “it’s never going to change how you feel at work”. One key finding of the study is “if people want to hang on to their talent, they really need to do something about their culture”. More broadly, the Anthro-LawSoc Legal Profession Sustainability study, conducted with the Law Society of Singapore, highlights the pressures that have led to high attrition rates in the profession for decades. As its executive summary notes, speeches, studies and press coverage for the past 30 years “all point to the same troubles: high stress, heavy workloads, poor balance between work and life, and declining mental health”. Interventions including wellness programmes, mentoring and flexible work have not created much change: “Despite these efforts, the rate of lawyers leaving has continued to climb.” Issac’s report suggests a range of system-wide retention mechanisms, including moving away from billable hours, and meaningful flexible working patterns such as “viable part-time partner tracks”. While this survey was conducted in Singapore, the symptoms and structural issues are very similar for lawyers in the UK and elsewhere. Trish McLellan, interim CEO at LawCare, a charity supporting mental health in the UK legal sector, says the billing system is not in itself problematic, but urges legal leaders to take a wider view: “People focus on what they’re rewarded for. If billable hours and target achievement are valued above everything else, it’s no surprise people feel they have to keep working, even when they’re exhausted. We need to think more broadly — good client care, teamwork, supporting and helping others develop all matter too, but they’re often less well valued and rewarded.” One change that would help shift things? “Our research found that many managers have never had any training. That’s something we need to change,” Trish says. The underlying issue is that humans aren’t built for sustained stress, which is exactly what lawyers (and others in high-stakes professional environments) either have to endure. Simon Gilbody, professor of psychology and epidemiology at the University of York, outlines what happens to us: “Our brains evolved to respond to immediate threats, such as predators, conflict, or physical danger, rather than the chronic, psychologically loaded pressures of modern life in the law. A demanding high-pressure legal workplace will repeatedly activate the same threat systems that once protected our hunter-gatherer ancestors 🦁.” Lawyers with brains in “a constant state of vigilance and arousal” don’t perform well, Simon says: “This works against concentration, decision-making and emotional regulation. These are the very capacities that lawyers rely upon, so that’s bad for individuals and for organisations.” Attrition in this environment is inevitable, but “losing talent costs money”. * In a nutshell: We know that humans can’t cope with sustained stress, and yet that’s how law firms (and many other corporates) are often structured. Will attrition rates become so high — with AI a new source of stress and uncertainty — that something finally changes? * Want more? LawCare’s Life in the Law 2025 report has lots of recommendations for more sustainable careers and corporate structures. FIVE TOP STORIES FROM THE WORLD OF WORK ‌ ‌ 1. Advantage, Wall Street? Why finance firms seek sports stars for advice: Elite sportspeople are being paid for their expertise — Novak Djokovic is “global strategic adviser” at a private equity company, while Serena Williams has started her own VC firm. Emma Jacobs investigates. 2. The reality check of leaving the abstract world of finance: Craig Coben’s column about life after a City career examines the consequences of the fact that “finance professionals model reality more than they deal with it”. 3. What’s that smell in the office? Pilita Clark examines the fragrant world of bespoke corporate scents, including finance offices and upmarket airport lounges. FT commenters would rather have fresh air 💨. 4. Everyone loves apprenticeships. So why can’t Britain create more of them? Professor Alison Wolf asks the question that many want answered in a Weekend essay. We could learn a lot by looking at the success of apprenticeships in the past, she says. 5. The great AI data centre cover-up: More great writing from Pilita Clark, this time explaining how “data hubs already devour more electricity globally than all but 10 countries” — and there’s a lot more environmental misery to come. It’s a vital read. ONE MORE THING . . . ‌ ‌ Derek Thompson has a fascinating Substack newsletter, and this week looks at “what a forgotten 100-year-old [US] government report says about who we are”. Some of the insights are timeless: as Derek writes, “The watchword of the day was balance. Appearing 30 times in the Recent Social Trends report, balance was the cardinal worry of economic commentators: balance between rural and urban America; between manufacturing and farming; and between rapid progress and traditional values.” OFFICE THERAPY ‌ ‌ The problem: We have a huge client deadline to meet — but an issue with capacity in our team. We need guidance on prioritising, support with AI training and rollout — and a sign-off to buy in help from trusted contractors. Unfortunately the department head is a bully, won’t sign off budget for outside help, isn’t guiding the AI rollout — and blames us for everything that falls short 😞. Previously we’ve managed workloads and dealt with issues among ourselves or by “back channels”. Now, though, the wider business is wholly preoccupied with AI transformation. Our manager has left us to implement that, on top of our normal workload. How to proceed when you have a manager who works against their team, not with them? Isabel’s reply: I despair of workplace advice that suggests you can get a result with a bad manager by speaking directly to them, getting advice from someone senior, or going to HR. (There’s a pile of optimistic leadership books on my desk — but what about the people actively working against “belonging”, or who’d scoff at “high-agency teams”? 🤷‍♀️) Try the conventional tactics: talk to people who might be able to help, and ask team members to keep a record of the manager’s bullying and obstruction. Beyond that, the AI rollout is a chance to effect change. Ask for help and training from whoever is in charge 🙋‍♀️. Be specific about your needs. Don’t make it about the manager — focus on the wider transformation, and stay positive in your interactions. The outcome your team seeks is likely aligned with that of the CEO and senior leaders: AI-powered efficiency and a company-wide focus on clearly stated priorities. Could you get the extra funding in this context? You will also be shown to be curious, proactive, collaborative: all the qualities that we are told will be key in future workplaces. But keep those notes about the manager’s behaviour, and keep talking as a team. Lack of support and outright bullying from a boss is profoundly upsetting for affected staff — but also bad for business. Someone will eventually choose to acknowledge that, and you’ve got the receipts🤞🏼. body: **************************************** Build a Free CRM with Formspree + Notion **************************************** Most leads go cold the same way. Someone fills out your form, you get an email, you mean to follow up, then a week or more passes. So long sales opportunity. The fix isn't Salesforce or HubSpot — you'd be paying $50-$100 /month for a contact timeline and lead scoring engine you'll never touch. As soon as someone hits submit, they should be in your pipeline. No spreadsheets, no subscriptions. That's Formspree + Notion. What it looks like in practice When someone submits your form, a new row appears in your Notion database automatically — name, email, company, message, timestamp, and a status field that starts at "New" so you know it requires action. Switch to board view and drag contacts from New > Contacted > Qualified as you work through them. It's a visual pipeline, built entirely in Notion. subject: The United States’ dream didn’t die. It was overturned
body:
SEATTLE — With pink cleats in his left hand, Folarin Balogun took a long, solitary trudge out of this World Cup. It took him two minutes to walk from the center circle to the tunnel, away from the firestorm. With all he had to process, it must have felt like two lifetimes.

He lowered his head, but he paused every few steps to look up and clap his right hand against his left thumb to acknowledge the thinning crowd at Seattle Stadium. He continued the routine until he was out of sight, a man fluctuating between sorrow and gratitude.

Said Balogun: “The feeling of disappointment is very difficult to put into words, I think, for me.”
